title: ResNet
matchup: He et al. (December 2015) vs Srivastava, Greff & Schmidhuber (May 2015) and Hochreiter (1991)
question: Do the earlier Highway Networks and recurrent connections establish the residual-network priority that Schmidhuber claims?

usual_credit.summary: Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren and Jian Sun at Microsoft Research introduced deep residual learning in December 2015, using identity shortcut connections so that layers learn residual functions, and won the ILSVRC 2015 ImageNet classification contest with networks of up to 152 layers. Residual connections have since become a standard component of convolutional networks and Transformers.

claim.summary: Schmidhuber says the ResNet is a Highway Network, introduced seven months earlier by Srivastava, Greff and himself, whose gates are always open, and that Highway Networks were the first working feedforward networks with hundreds of layers. He adds that residual connections with weight 1.0 go back to Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis and to the constant error flow of LSTM, that the ResNet paper calls the Highway Network 'concurrent' although it appeared first, and that it cites Bengio et al. (1994) for vanishing gradients but not Hochreiter (1991).

quotes.text: Setting all Highway NN gates to 1.0 effectively gives us the ResNet published 7 months later.
The ResNet paper[HW2] calls our earlier Highway Net[HW1] "concurrent," but it wasn't: the ResNet was published 7 months later.
Sepp Hochreiter introduced residual connections for recurrent NNs (RNNs) in a diploma thesis (June 1991)[VAN1] supervised by Jürgen Schmidhuber
A follow-up paper by the ResNet authors suffered from design flaws leading to incorrect conclusions about gated residual connections.[HW25b]

response.summary: He and colleagues cite both Highway Network papers but distinguish their ungated identity shortcuts from data-dependent, parameterized gates. Their 2016 follow-up reports that several multiplicative shortcut designs hamper optimization in very deep networks. Highway Network co-author Rupesh Srivastava [disputes that comparison](https://rupeshks.cc/blog/skip.html), arguing that its highway implementation has design mistakes. Lucas Beyer, an outside commentator, questions the word concurrent while regarding the ungated result as useful evidence. These positions separate a mathematical open-gate limit from the empirical question of which network trains well; the papers do not answer the separate 1991-thesis citation complaint.

agreed_facts: Srivastava, Greff and Schmidhuber posted 'Highway Networks' on arXiv on 3 May 2015, and 'Training Very Deep Networks' on 22 July 2015.
He et al. posted 'Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition' on arXiv on 10 December 2015 and report that their 152-layer network won first place in the ILSVRC 2015 classification task.
The ResNet paper cites both Highway Network papers and calls them 'concurrent'.
The ResNet paper cites Bengio, Simard and Frasconi (1994) for the vanishing and exploding gradient problem, and it does not cite Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis.
Hochreiter's diploma thesis was written at TU Munich in 1991 under Schmidhuber and analyzes vanishing and exploding error signals in recurrent networks.
He et al. posted 'Identity Mappings in Deep Residual Networks' in March 2016, and it cites the Highway Network papers.
crux: The dispute is over whether an identity-shortcut network with no gates is a distinct design from a gated Highway Network or simply its open-gate limit, and whether a December 2015 paper should have treated a May 2015 preprint as prior work instead of 'concurrent'. A further question is whether the weight-1.0 recurrent connection of Hochreiter's 1991 thesis and of LSTM is the same idea as a residual connection between layers.

card.headline: Residual networks (ResNet)
card.question: Is ResNet essentially a Highway Network with its gates held open?
card.claim: He says ResNet is a Highway Network whose gates are always open, published seven months later, and that residual connections date to Hochreiter's 1991 thesis.
card.pushback: He et al. report that gating the shortcuts hampers training of very deep networks, and that Highway Networks had not shown gains past 100 layers.
card.crux: The question is whether a network without gates is a new design or the open-gate special case of Highway Networks.
